title: Conjecture 3.4
statement_text: $t(n)=n-2$ if and only if $n$ is prime.
context_text: A cyclic permutation of order $n$ is an arrangement of $1,\dots,n$ on a circle, up to rotation; equivalently, with $c=(1,2,\dots,n)\in S_n$ and $C_n=\langle c\rangle$, it is a coset $[\pi]=\pi C_n$ of a permutation $\pi\in S_n$. The sorting time $t([\pi])$ is the minimum number of swaps of two (not necessarily adjacent) entries needed to transform $[\pi]$ into the trivial cyclic permutation $[c]$, and $t(n)=\max_{\pi\in S_n}t([\pi])$ is the diameter of the (vertex-transitive) graph on cyclic permutations of order $n$ in which two are adjacent when they differ by one swap. Writing $\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma)$ for the number of cycles of $\sigma\in S_n$, one has $t([\pi])=\min_{\sigma\in\pi C_n}(n-\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma))$. Since every permutation has a cyclic shift with a fixed point, $t(n)\le n-2$. For $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n^\times$ (the units of $\mathbb{Z}_n$), let $\pi_{n,a}\in S_n$ be the permutation $i\mapsto a\cdot i \pmod n$ (identifying $[n]$ with $\mathbb{Z}_n$). Using $\pi_{n,g}$ for a suitable generator $g$, the authors prove $t(p^k)\ge p^k-k-1$ for every odd prime $p$, hence $t(n)=n-2$ for every prime $n$; they also prove $t(n)\ge n-O(\log n)$ in general. Computer experiments show that for $n\le 11$ the upper bound $n-2$ is attained only for prime $n$, so the conjecture is that the converse also holds. It would follow from the stronger conjecture that if $n>2$ and $\max_{\sigma\in\pi C_n}\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma)=2$ then $n$ is prime and $\pi=\pi_{n,a}$ for some $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n^\times$; both have been verified for $n\le11$.

title: Conjecture 3.6
statement_text: If $n>2$ and $\pi\in S_n$ satisfies $\max_{\sigma\in\pi C_n}\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma)=2$, then $n$ is prime and $\pi(i)\equiv a\cdot i \pmod n$ for all $i$, for some $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n^\times$.

The conjecture characterizes the extremal permutations as the multiplication maps $\pi_{n,a}$ (the hypothesis depends only on the coset $\pi C_n$ while the conclusion, as literally stated in the paper, depends on the representative $\pi$, since $\pi_{n,a}c^j$ is $i\mapsto a(i+j)$; presumably $[\pi]=[\pi_{n,a}]$ is meant). It implies the conjecture that $t(n)=n-2$ if and only if $n$ is prime, and both conjectures have been verified for $n\le 11$.

title: Question 3.9
context_text: A cyclic permutation of order $n$ is an arrangement of $1,\dots,n$ on a circle, up to rotation; equivalently, with $c=(1,2,\dots,n)\in S_n$ and $C_n=\langle c\rangle$, it is a coset $[\pi]=\pi C_n$ of a permutation $\pi\in S_n$. The sorting time $t([\pi])$ is the minimum number of swaps of two (not necessarily adjacent) entries needed to transform $[\pi]$ into the trivial cyclic permutation $[c]$, and $t(n)=\max_{\pi\in S_n}t([\pi])$ is the diameter of the (vertex-transitive) graph on cyclic permutations of order $n$ in which two are adjacent when they differ by one swap. Writing $\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma)$ for the number of cycles of $\sigma\in S_n$, one has $t([\pi])=\min_{\sigma\in\pi C_n}(n-\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma))$. Since every permutation has a cyclic shift with a fixed point, $t(n)\le n-2$. For $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n^\times$ (the units of $\mathbb{Z}_n$), let $\pi_{n,a}\in S_n$ be the permutation $i\mapsto a\cdot i \pmod n$ (identifying $[n]$ with $\mathbb{Z}_n$). Using $\pi_{n,g}$ for a suitable generator $g$, the authors prove $t(p^k)\ge p^k-k-1$ for every odd prime $p$, hence $t(n)=n-2$ for every prime $n$; they also prove $t(n)\ge n-O(\log n)$ in general. For powers of 2 they show $t(2^k)\ge 2^k-(2k-1)$ for $k\ge3$, and for $n=2p^k$ ($p$ an odd prime) $t(n)\ge n-2k-2$. If $t(n)$ were monotone, these bounds for prime powers could be transferred to other integers. However, adding a fixed point to a permutation may decrease its sorting time: $t([\pi_{11,3}])=9$, while extending $\pi_{11,3}$ to $S_{12}$ by fixing $12$ gives sorting time $8$.
